name: Music NFT Era — A scene, in the making
description: Build a scrolling music documentary from original sources, artist stories and playable NFT artifacts—with a reusable research and production recipe.
about:
Music NFT Era grew out of Pete Rango’s effort to document a scene through the people, music and experiments that made it matter. Working with Codex, he kept pushing the project beyond a catalog of platforms and releases: what were artists trying to change, how did people find one another, and what did they carry forward?

The early version felt too much like a wiki. Pete wanted the story to unfold as you scrolled, with photographs, original artwork and short passages that gave each moment room. That changed the structure into a documentary with optional deeper chapters. The opening took several passes: isolated dates and unexplained artist references gave way to context about making, funding and collecting music, followed by a deliberate step back into the earlier experiments.

The writing changed just as much. Pete rejected fact-by-fact narration and asked for a music journalist’s account of the whole era. The rewrite connected artist agency, collective work and participation, rather than letting prices, drops or platform milestones tell the story. Research widened to builders, organizers, collaborators and music videos. Grok conversations generated leads; original interviews, release pages, journals and event records supplied evidence. Later, the Minted transcript opened further research into LATASHÁ’s motivations and work. Pete also pulled back an over-expansion into a separate filmmaker chapter: collaborators should be discoverable without taking the music out of focus.

Reviewing the experience exposed what a reader still couldn’t do. Names needed faces, context and work you could hear. People and project links became contextual profiles; listening moved onto the artwork, with a persistent queue. Missing contributor releases and an overemphasis on CHAOS prompted broader coverage and collection filters. Pete’s request to recover Sound releases, including Optimism, and The Park’s archive led to chain and metadata research—with unresolved originals left visible as gaps instead of invented players.

The result is a selected cultural history and listening archive, shaped through research, editorial rewrites and repeated desktop and phone reviews. The build record below preserves those decisions and the reusable prompts; reconstructed prompts are labeled, not presented as a verbatim conversation. This edition records 232 selected recordings, not a complete history or discography. It uses source-backed editorial data and read-only token metadata, not writes to Music Nerd’s knowledge database. Image-use review, missing media and collection coverage remain open. The public repository branch predates parts of the deployed working copy, so cloning it alone does not reproduce every later iteration.

# Prompts and steering

These are reusable prompts reconstructed from the task and its iterations. They are not claimed to be the exact full prompts sent in every prior tool or Grok session. Original meeting transcripts are not reproduced here.

## Starting brief

> Build a working, source-backed documentary about the Music NFT era for someone who was not there and someone who was. Start from a small slice that goes deep: people, releases, gatherings, experiments and evidenced connections. Research before designing. Inspect 6–8 relevant digital exhibitions and music experiences, including actual desktop/mobile behavior. Research the history through original releases, artist accounts, interviews and event records. Separate verified facts, attributed memories and interpretation.
>
> Build separately from MusicNerdWeb, under Documents/Music Nerd, using existing supported Music Nerd APIs only where appropriate. Do not create a speculative knowledge backend or expose private Lore. A clearly labeled source-backed local fixture is acceptable. Do not merge, deploy, purchase services or change production data.
>
> Make the experience an immersive editorial music archive. Let scrolling immediately carry the visitor into the story. Explain what music NFTs were and why artists explored them before requiring prior knowledge. Use expressive, correctly attributed imagery, readable short passages, deliberate changes of composition and restrained motion. No autoplay sound, scroll hijacking, wallet-first entry or decorative graph clouds.
>
> Provide a curated 6–8 minute reading path with optional depth. A visitor can hear work, follow a meaningful connection, inspect its evidence and return without losing their place. Give every named participant a way to be understood through a profile, documented role, work or verified public links. Test the actual browser experience on desktop and phone, including keyboard, reduced motion, failures, history and listening.

## Research interviewer: open discovery

> Investigate music NFTs as a cultural history, without beginning from a supplied artist roster. Find communities, genres, regions, organizers and experiments that are missing from the familiar platform narrative. For each candidate scene: who did what, when, why, what was actually made, what participation meant, what happened afterward, and what remains uncertain. Supply original source URLs, dates and identifiable releases. Distinguish announcement from outcome, billing from attendance, and a transaction from a relationship. Seek disagreement and ordinary organizing work as well as successes. Do not let prices or fundraising dominate the account.

## Research interviewer: follow an existing lead

> For [person/project], reconstruct three concrete scenes using original posts, releases, event records and recorded interviews. Who else did the work? What mechanics were tried? How did participants experience them? What changed or failed? Find original artifacts and exact chain/contract/token references where available. Challenge contradictions in counts, dates and credits. Label participant recollections, contemporary documents and later interpretation. Do not invent missing links or turn plans into completed outcomes.

Grok was used as a lead generator in two threads, one seeded and one initially open. Its answers were not used as primary evidence. The public sources are the reproducible resource; recreating private browser sessions is unnecessary.

## Important steering that changed the result

- Replace the wiki/dashboard feeling with a visual scrolling documentary; do not become attached to the initial layout.
- Use the other local documentary as an interaction reference, but create an independent identity. Wodniack was a motion reference; do not copy its interactive banner.
- Give enough context to complete a thought. An isolated 2015 title card or an unexplained Daniel Allan opening was insufficient.
- Cover Catalog's builders, Songcamp/CHAOS, Sound, Mint Songs, Zora and Glass alongside artists and organizers. Follow music videos, not only audio editions.
- Preserve the cultural frame: the moments, participants, collaboration, experiments, questions and outcomes.
- Put play directly on artwork. Replace the separate listening modal/native-player stack with a persistent collection queue and direct listening.
- Preload one upcoming recording to reduce skip latency; avoid loading all media.
- Treat names as entry points into people. Verify aliases, preserve historical credits, and offer external profiles only when supported.
- End with what participants carried forward, including Pete's explicitly attributed reflection on building tools for one's community. Do not universalize that recollection.

## Verification prompt

> Run the implementation. Follow the whole path at desktop and phone widths. Open a named person's drawer, follow their source and return; verify the exact scroll position and focus. Play, pause, skip, shuffle and inspect the queue; verify one active audio stream and bounded preloading. Distinguish mocked player tests from live auditions. Inspect real screenshots for cropped faces, unreadable text, stale scene frames, busy controls and overflow. Correct failures before calling the preview ready.


---

# Actual process and reproducible method

1. **Inspect context and boundaries.** Read applicable project instructions, existing screens and the meeting brief. Use the private November 3 record only for intent; its speaker labels do not establish individual authorship. Keep this standalone and preserve dirty workspaces. Locate the owning issue before repository work.
2. **Observe reference experiences.** Record the actual interface inspected, viewport, interaction, evidence and weakness. Separate visited behavior from a search result or promotional image. Translate the lesson into a design decision; do not copy identity or assets. See the reference matrix in `docs/RESEARCH.md`.
3. **Build an evidence ledger.** Store original URL, author, publication/event date, claim supported, evidence type and limitation. Research independently of the supplied roster, then investigate named gaps. Fetch original public documents where possible. Private Docs must not go through public scraping services.
4. **Follow artifacts and credits.** A source can identify a release, which supplies contributors, which leads to another credited work. Ownership supplies transaction evidence only. Retain alternate names and conflicting counts. A release announcement is not an outcome.
5. **Write a complete thought before arranging a scene.** Establish the artist's stakes; explain the mechanism through an actual work; show what people did; leave a route into more detail. The current frame follows changing participation rather than a sequence of platform funding rounds.
6. **Compose the documentary.** Use the existing approved visual system, full-frame photography, contained original artworks, varied passage positions and native-scroll crossfades. Keep evidence and longer branches optional. Use real captions so a portrait never masquerades as an event photograph.
7. **Connect listening.** Verify an allowlisted contract/token using the read-only adapter, read metadata and follow original media. Use a play control on artwork and a persistent queue. Cached artwork derivatives are for display; do not replace the original recording with an unverified reupload.
8. **Connect people.** A canonical profile can have historical aliases, a brief source-backed introduction, release credits, related moments and verified external links. Names in editorial text open the existing drawer. Unknown biography is a gap, not an invitation to invent influence. Metadata-derived collaborator records are labeled as credits.
9. **Run behavioral checks and inspect the result.** Validate references and security boundaries, then browser navigation, focus, reduced motion, themes, queue and failures. Inspect captures rather than equating a passing test with aesthetic acceptance. Keep live-media availability distinct from controlled tests.
10. **Package the knowledge.** Record decisions, source paths, prompts, reproduction commands and remaining dependencies. Update the Lab submission packet; do not publish merely because the packet exists.

The workflow used repository reads and edits, public web research, Firecrawl source retrieval, Grok interviews through the user's browser, Ethereum metadata reads, image asset conversion, and Playwright verification. Tool vendors are replaceable; their evidentiary roles are not. Public research caches are disposable; curated sources and the distinctions they support must remain tracked.

## Integrated documentary pass — November 4

The main film now connects the search for agency to learning in public, community release experiments, and the work of keeping access alive. New optional chapters cover Erin Ivey and Mint Songs, LNRZ/Sara Phillips, and CAMPFIRE Miami; expanded Heart Project and Black Dave/Glass passages distinguish announcements from demonstrated outcomes. The Park anchors the aftermath before Pete's attributed builder reflection. Definitions distinguish a unique token from a copyable recording.

The library contains 218 selected representative recordings, including 22 newly recovered Optimism V1 releases and two legacy Sound releases. Discovery found 1,787 Optimism V1 release contracts and 172 legacy artist contracts; these are inventories, not counts of imported songs or proof of exhaustive coverage. Legacy indexing remains retryable after public API rate limits. See sound-legacy-coverage.md and SOUND-PARK-IMPORT.md.

Playback now retries the identical IPFS content address through a second fixed gateway on failure, buffers the next track, and lets individual collection editions enter the queue without losing full-precision token IDs. This does not restore unavailable content. Correction links open a prefilled GitHub issue draft; visitors choose whether to submit.

Portraits added for Imogen Heap (CC BY-SA with attribution), Erin Ivey and Nate Mercereau (artist-distributed press sources). Direct license links and crop/source captions are preserved. The image audit records the actual evidence rather than implying every image has blanket publication clearance.

# Decisions that shaped the experience

This is a reconstruction of observed iterations, not a complete chronological transcript. Dates are only assigned where the edit is recorded.

| Decision | What prompted it | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Separate repository | Music Nerd is the knowledge layer; the artifact should stand independently | Read-only adapters and editorial fixtures rather than a new knowledge backend |
| Scrolling documentary | Initial directory/wiki layout required clicks before the story began | Six movements unfold on native scroll, with optional branches |
| Human stakes before the early date | An isolated 2015 licensing example did not complete the opening thought | Explain agency and collecting, then step back into selected precursors; no definitive-first claim |
| Original art and accurate captions | Initials, absent visuals and cropped portraits weakened the experience | Responsive imagery, deliberate framing, original token artwork and explicit source captions |
| Direct artwork play | Separate listening modal and native audio controls felt cumbersome | Direct play controls plus persistent collection queue |
| One-track prebuffer | Skipping waited on repeated metadata/media lookup | Silently prepare only the upcoming recording; keep request scope bounded |
| Culture beyond drops | Coverage missed organizers, ordinary participation and artist experiments | Future Surf, artist worlds, filmed performances and changing participation supply deeper branches |
| Names open people | Full names alone still left participants unexplained | Shared contextual drawer, evidence, recordings and verified external links |
| Aliases remain historical | Pete identified Aly as Lackhoney; a contemporary newsletter links the names | Shared person context and search; original titles/credits preserved |
| Lab build record | Pete requested a recreatable protocol | This versioned packet records prompts, process, resources, tests and limits |

An alternative considered and rejected: adding every possible navigation mode or a decorative relationship graph. Connections should first work through a specific person, artifact and source. Broader history remains expandable without bloating the primary reading path.

## Context at the point of discovery · November 4

Pete flagged unexplained Imogen Heap and Zora references. Added a full Tiny Human passage with Heap’s illustrated song map, its later publication date, the licensing/payment experiment and Ujo’s closure explanation. Platform/project names now reuse the same accessible, history-aware drawer as people. Period-specific entries distinguish Zora’s marketplace, shared infrastructure and gatherings; Catalog, Sound, Glass, Loft Radio, Mycelia, Ujo and Zoratopia also have context. Click/tap gives full context; the link title supplies a brief desktop hover hint. Avoid hover-only information. These are editorial fixtures, not new live Music Nerd integrations.

## Coverage and discovery correction · November 4, midday

Pete flagged missing portraits, past-tense NFT definitions, CHAOS dominating the general recordings page, and absent contributor outputs. Removed the CHAOS spotlight from the general library (its story-specific chapter remains); CHAOS is available through the Collections filter. Artist filtering and text search now include source-confirmed contributor identities. Present-tense definitions distinguish the medium from dated events. Four public profile images and four direct-token-verified recordings were added. The research ledger now lists image and recording coverage for every person rather than implying the partial index is a complete discography. CAMPFIRE announcements with unresolved contracts remain evidence links, not fabricated players.

## November 4 · experience refinement

After the coverage audit, the next pass prioritized discovering and hearing work inside artist context. Profile drawers reuse compact recording cards (up to three selected works), place them before source lists, and stop their inline player when the drawer closes or changes. A player in the underlying library remains intact during a profile detour. Role credits distinguish production from performance and ownership. Reduced profile-image and library-header sizes keep the next useful action visible. Browser inspection exposed blank areas during remote artwork loading; five verified token artworks now have local responsive WebP derivatives. Original audio/video URLs remain unchanged. The closing passage now separates surviving tokens, media, websites and community rather than treating a closed platform as the end of NFTs.

## November 4 · whole-documentary editorial rewrite

Pete rejected fact-by-fact narration and requested a music-journalist’s synthesis across the entire experience. Rewrote the 18 film passages and 36 deeper chapter bodies around agency, participation, collective work and afterlives. Retained dates and source/uncertainty records; kept uncertainty in the narration where it changes the story. Added paragraph pacing, removed empty generic sidebars, and made Future Surf’s named hosts actual participant links. New synthesis used the existing research, not newly claimed interviews. See `docs/EDITORIAL-APPROACH.md` and the exported script. A source-backed argument is required; confident tone alone is not sufficient.

## November 4: Sound discovery, Park reconciliation and manual listening queue

User requested all Sound NFTs, specifically Optimism, and supplied The Park's works archive. Added reproducible read-only factory-log discovery, explicit missing-metadata state, cross-chain token readers and ERC1155 URI support. Audited the artist's public release pages separately from chain verification. Imported only recovered representative NFT records; left unresolved records in the coverage inventory. Added chain filtering and card-level queue actions using the existing player. See `../research/SOUND-PARK-IMPORT.md` for commands, exact scope and remaining completeness gaps. Neither the factory inventory nor the Park source list is advertised as a complete NFT archive.

## November 4: terminology, interpretation and verification

Pete asked to define non-fungible and token, and move ahead on the broader gaps. The first definition was too dense on mobile; it became two short editorial definitions within the existing opening. Clarified that music can be copied and that the token carries distinct identity/history, rather than claiming an NFT prevents copying. Added The Park's optional source-backed chapter with three playable records and a route to all 29 imported works. Expanded older Sound factory discovery using official deployment artifacts, rather than extrapolating from V2. Added a bounded shared metadata-request cache; failed reads remain retryable. The image audit distinguishes attribution, official press distribution and unverified licenses; it does not treat protected hosting as copyright clearance.

# Run and verify a recreation

Repository: `https://github.com/xdjs/music-nft-era`. Current working copy: `<project-root>`.

The local working copy contains changes beyond the remote branch. A future builder must use a reviewed commit containing this packet and the corresponding implementation; do not assume an older remote checkout reproduces the latest preview.

```sh
npm ci
npm start
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:4178/`. Node requirement is in `package.json` (currently 22+). This is a vanilla JavaScript/CSS app with a Node server, not a Next.js app. No production database migration is needed.

```sh
npm run ci
```

This runs syntax checks, formatting, unit tests and Playwright browser tests. Install the Playwright browser if the environment does not already have it. Do not weaken a check or substitute a mock result for a live claim.

## Observable acceptance

- Scrolling starts the story without a required click; context explains music NFTs and artist motivations.
- Optional chapters and sources return to the same reading position.
- Named people open contextual profiles; source and social links are distinguishable; aliases preserve original credits.
- Original NFT recordings play from artwork, with a persistent collection player, queue, skip, shuffle and one-track prebuffering.
- CHAOS songs and collectible editions can be explored separately; recording filters compose and deep-link.
- Keyboard focus, Escape, Back and reduced motion behave coherently; no phone-width overflow.
- Failed metadata/directory/media requests offer understandable recovery rather than a fake empty success.
- No private file, credential or write endpoint becomes public.

Live playback depends on RPC and original storage availability. The browser suite controls some media responses. Audition representative live audio/video separately and report unavailable originals honestly. The current reader supports allowlisted Ethereum, Optimism, Base and Zora records; chain and token references must be verified independently.

## Publishing or Lab submission

Prepare a concrete reviewed commit, rights review, preview URL and representative desktop/phone captures. Inspect Lab's actual submission fields when submission is requested. Map this packet into those fields. Publishing, deployment and merging require the user's authorization; this document does not supply it.

## Additional import and recovery implementation

- `scripts/sound-contracts.mjs` records verified Sound deployment generations. `scripts/import-sound.mjs` discovers edition contracts; `scripts/sound-legacy-import.mjs` groups legacy artist-contract purchase and mint events. Keep legacy artist counts separate from release counts. See `docs/research/sound-legacy-coverage.md` for evidence, invocations and limitations.
- Generated public modules are `src/sound-import-v1-10.js` and `src/sound-legacy-import.js`; unpublished checkpoints remain under `data/`. Expose only curated records through the static allowlist.
- `src/media-recovery.js` retries the same IPFS path once through a second fixed gateway. Unit and browser tests verify this boundary; no media reupload is involved.
- The main script can be inspected in `docs/EDITORIAL-SCRIPT-2026-11-04.md`; optional branches live in `src/narrative.js`.
- Run `npm run ci` (includes importer tests) and restart the local Node server after modifying its file allowlist. Verify actual original-media availability separately from mocked playback.

# Resource and implementation map

## Historical evidence

- `src/data.js` and `src/narrative.js`: the actual source records, moments, people, relationships and optional close readings used by the site.
- `docs/SOURCES.md`, `docs/ERA-RESEARCH-LEDGER.md`, `docs/STORY-EDIT-2026-11-04.md`: source inventory, expansion leads and latest editorial decisions.
- `src/nft-catalog.js`: selected chain/contract/token editions, original artwork pointers, credits and checked-block metadata. A selection, not an artist's complete discography.
- `docs/NFT-COVERAGE.md`, `docs/MEDIA.md`, `docs/PEOPLE-IMAGES.md`: coverage and image attribution/limitations.

Primary starting points: Songcamp journals and the Walls oral history; Catalog founder interviews; artist release notes; Sound announcements; Zoratopia event records; Future Surf newsletters; TK's Digital Punks interview; Black Dave's Glass/Reveel essay; original Heart Project updates; Violetta Zironi's Moonshot page; the Chill Pill retrospective; Coop Records founder accounts. Exact links and dates are in the source records, not reconstructed from handles.

## Design and implementation

- `docs/CINEMATIC-DIRECTION.md`, `docs/DESIGN.md`, `docs/RESEARCH.md`: visual decisions, reference behavior and its adaptation.
- `src/app.js`: routing, scrolling scenes, drawer/history behavior, inline listening, recording filters and contextual name links.
- `src/film.css`: current documentary treatment. `src/style.css`: shared pages, controls and drawers.
- `src/playlist.js`: persistent queue, playback state, skip/shuffle and one-upcoming-track buffering.
- `src/nft-reader.mjs`: original-token metadata/media resolution and URL boundaries.
- `src/nft-collections.mjs`: collection browsing adapter.
- `src/directory.js`: constrained Music Nerd identity lookup.
- `server.mjs`: local server and explicit public-file allowlist. Adding a browser module/asset requires updating it.
- `tests/`: data-edge checks, adapter boundaries and browser journeys.

## Access and rights

Local source-backed editorial fixtures are sufficient to reproduce the journey without a production database. Live Music Nerd checks are limited to independently pinned identities. No private Lore, raw internal research or credentials belong in the client or protocol.

A public source is not a blanket asset license. Preserve attribution and provenance, use lawful embeds, and review rights before public distribution. Local contextual artwork use and verification of its original token address do not confer publication rights.

The original private meeting Doc, authenticated Grok conversation state and raw working transcripts are not part of this public packet. Keep their lessons and public citations, not private payloads.

instructions:
Help me build my own music exhibition, inspired by Music NFT Era. Start by asking one question at a time and waiting for my answer. Use what I have already told you. Offer concrete choices when I am unsure.

First ask what scene, community, artist or experiment I want to explore, and why it matters to me. Then find out who the experience is for; what visitors should understand, hear or do; the period and scope; my starting sources and recordings; preferred languages and devices; visual references and available brand assets; and my time, budget and technical comfort. Do not assume my subject involves NFTs or needs a blockchain.

Summarize a small first edition and get my agreement before researching or building.

Research original artist accounts, releases, interviews, gathering records and credits. Treat AI conversations as leads to check, not evidence. Preserve source URLs, dates, disagreements, missing voices and uncertainty. Distinguish announcements from outcomes, ownership from collaboration, and platform closure from the end of a community.

Propose a documentary path that completes thoughts and explains unfamiliar terms. Focus on people, work and participation. Offer optional depth without making people click through a directory before the story begins. Agree the story and a representative visual section before building the whole site. Inspect my existing design system and references; use permitted assets and accurate captions.

Put listening where it advances the story. Use legitimate embeds or verified original media with provider links and honest failure states. If token-based work belongs in my story, verify chain, contract and token references and explain what ownership does and does not imply. Keep metadata lookup read-only. Do not require a wallet to read or listen.

Use contextual profiles, sources and optional chapters only where useful. Preserve reading position and focus when returning. If a queue is needed, keep one active player and bounded preloading. Avoid autoplay sound and scroll hijacking.

Choose the simplest stack that fits the agreed brief. Keep secrets on the server, make failed external requests retryable, and distinguish local fixtures from live integrations. Do not invent a Music Nerd backend or claim account sync without a supported, tested integration.

Review actual desktop and phone layouts, keyboard access, reduced motion, imagery, navigation and listening. Separate mocked tests from real playback; record unavailable media and unverified checks. Keep a cookbook of tools, research decisions and iterations. Help me prepare deployment, asking before publishing or using paid services.

Begin with: “What music community or experiment would you like people to step inside—and what should they take away?”
tools_used: Codex; public web research and Firecrawl; Grok for research leads; original artist/release/event sources; Node.js and vanilla JavaScript/CSS; Ethereum, Optimism, Base and Zora RPC reads; Blockscout indexing; IPFS/Arweave media; Playwright; Vercel. Source-backed local fixtures and live read-only metadata are kept distinct.
